To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) intranasal vaccination of mice increases the number of resident CD4+ effectors, 2) challenge with virulent F. tularensis increases the numbers of resident and circulating CD4+ effctors, 3) resident CD4+ T effector cells are superior at controlling infection, 4) circulating CD4+T effector cells control replication of F. tularensic in vitro, 5) circulating CD4 T cells are required for early control,

pulmonary infection with a highly virulent intracelluar bacterium is controlled by both tissue-resident and circulating T cells, with the tissue-resident cells providing a dominant response in vivo but with the circulating cells superior for in vitro control of bacterial replication.
the lung has distinct anatomical pools of T cells with specific functions that are required at specific time points to clear a highly virulent intrapulmonary infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the generation and function of T cells that are generated by vaccination and subsequently respond during infection.
the generation and maintenance of immunity by distinct T cell populations during pulmonary infection.
how the immune system controls infections with intracellular bacteria.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
pulmonary resident T cells are critical for controlling F. tularensis infection in a manner that is dependent upon the duration of the infection.
the lung has a complex and unique microenvironment that dictates the generation and maintenance of distinct T cell populations.
the lung has anatomically distinct T cell pools that play specific roles during infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
during the course of an Ftt infection in immune animals, the lung parenchymal pool of CD4 T cells expands and is the dominant effector pool.

during a pulmonary F. tularensis infection, the lung-resident CD4 T cells are the dominant effector cells that are responsible for the control of infection, while the circulating CD4 T cells play a critical role in maintaining the immune response in the lung and are superior at controlling intrabacterial replication.
the lung has distinct pools of T lymphocytes that play different roles in combating infection, and these roles are dependent on the kinetics of infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the lung is a complex immune organ with anatomically and functionally distinct T cell pools that play specific roles during pulmonary infection and that these roles are dependent on the kinetics of bacterial clearance.

the role of resident versus circulating T cells during pulmonary infection depends on the pathogen, and the immune response to a pathogen can change over the course of an infection, requiring the use of both populations for optimal control.
the timing of the infection dictates which pool of T cells is most important for the control of infection.
